explanations.answer: He is suddenly shattered beyond recovery
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The man who stays stiff-necked after much reproof will suddenly be shattered beyond recovery. Notice the word suddenly. I think it's a heavy line, and the plain lesson is that a stiff neck doesn't bend until it breaks. A cookie that won't give snaps in half the same way, and I've swept up plenty of those.

explanations.answer: He slowly learns his lesson over time
explanations.explanation: I get why that's tempting, because a slow lesson sounds gentler. But the proverb says this man will "suddenly be shattered beyond recovery." Nothing in the verse describes a slow climb toward wisdom. Think of a batch that sits fine in the oven and then, all at once, the smoke alarm goes off.

explanations.answer: He is given one more chance to listen
explanations.explanation: This man has already had much reproof, so the chances have been stacking up. The proverb doesn't mention one more. It says he will be shattered beyond recovery. Chances are a gift, friend, so don't leave them sitting on the counter.

Yes, friend. "When the righteous flourish, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan." Same people, two very different sounds. It tells you a lot about what a ruler does to everyone under him.

Dancing sounds like what rejoicing might look like. But rejoicing belongs to the first half, when the righteous flourish. When the wicked rule, the proverb says the people groan. I bet nobody's got dancing shoes on for that one.

The proverb never says a word about sleep. What it says is that the people groan when the wicked rule. I think a groaning crowd isn't sleeping much anyway. Rejoicing goes with the righteous flourishing, and groaning goes with the wicked ruling.

That's right. The companion of prostitutes squanders his wealth, while the man who loves wisdom brings joy to his father. Squander means it goes out the door and doesn't come back. This one's a serious picture, so I'll leave it at what the verse says.

Guarding wealth is the opposite of what the proverb says. The companion of prostitutes squanders it. Guarding is closer to the man who loves wisdom, though the verse says he brings joy to his father. Squanders is the word the text uses for the other man.

Doubling would be quite a deal, friend, and I'd have questions about the oven that did it. But the verse says this man squanders his wealth. It runs out instead of multiplying. The proverb has no good news about the money in this one.
Close, but it's flipped. The proverb says "By justice a king brings stability to the land." It's the man who exacts tribute who demolishes it. So he tears the land down instead of building it up.
Right, it's false. The proverb says a man who exacts tribute demolishes the land. Demolishes is a wrecking-ball word, friend. Stability comes from the king who rules by justice.

explanations.answer: Spreading a net for his feet
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. "A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his feet." The flattery looks like a compliment, but the proverb calls it a net. I'd keep my eyes open any time the praise gets extra thick.

explanations.answer: Building a wall around his house
explanations.explanation: A wall keeps trouble out. The proverb has a different picture, a net, and it's spread for his feet. Nothing in the verse says anything about a wall or a house. The flattery is the trap here.

explanations.answer: Planting a seed in his field
explanations.explanation: A seed grows into something good in a field, and that's a nice picture. But this proverb isn't about farming. It says the flatterer spreads a net for his feet. A net catches things, which is a very different kind of planting.
Yes, it's true. "An evil man is caught by his own sin." The same verse says the righteous one sings and rejoices. One man is stuck and the other is singing.
Actually the proverb says exactly that. "An evil man is caught by his own sin." His own sin is what catches him. The righteous one gets the singing and rejoicing in the second half of the verse.

explanations.answer: They have no regard for such concerns
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The righteous consider the cause of the poor, but the wicked have no regard for such concerns. One side stops and thinks about the poor, and the other doesn't give it a thought. That's the whole contrast in one verse.

explanations.answer: They plead for the poor at the city gate
explanations.explanation: Nothing in this proverb mentions a city gate or anyone pleading there. It says the wicked have no regard for such concerns. The ones who consider the cause of the poor are the righteous. I'd keep those two groups on their own sides, friend.

explanations.answer: They give a little and then move on
explanations.explanation: That would at least be something, but it isn't what the proverb says. The wicked have no regard for such concerns. No regard means the cause of the poor doesn't register with them at all. Giving a little and moving on isn't in the verse.
That's right. Mockers inflame a city, but the wise turn away anger. One group lights the fire and the other puts it out. I know which one I'd want living next door.
Rumors do spread fast, friend, but that isn't the word here. The wise turn away anger. The mockers are the ones inflaming the city, and the wise are the ones calming it down.
The proverb doesn't mention enemies at all. It says the wise turn away anger. The thing being turned aside is the heat itself, and the wise are the ones who do it.

explanations.answer: Raving and laughing with no resolution
explanations.explanation: That's the verse word for word. If a wise man goes to court with a fool, "there will be raving and laughing with no resolution." The wise man gets no clean ending out of it. Friend, I'd say that's a court date nobody enjoys, even with a front-row seat.

explanations.answer: A quick confession from the fool
explanations.explanation: A quick confession would wrap things up nicely, but the proverb says there will be no resolution. What fills the room is raving and laughing. The fool isn't confessing anything in this verse.

explanations.answer: A fast ruling for the wise man
explanations.explanation: I'd love that for him, but the verse doesn't say it. It says there will be raving and laughing with no resolution. Nothing gets settled, so there's no ruling to speed up. The wise man still has to deal with the fool.

Yes, it's true. "Men of bloodshed hate a blameless man, but the upright care for his life." This is a heavy one, so I'll just say it plainly. The proverb puts the upright on the side of caring for his life.
The proverb actually says it. The men of bloodshed hate a blameless man, "but the upright care for his life." It's a heavy verse. The upright stand on the caring side.

That's the one. A fool vents all his anger, but a wise man holds it back. I've been the fool in this verse more than once, and the dough wasn't any better for it. Holding it back is what the proverb gives the wise man.
Later is still venting, friend. The proverb says the wise man holds it back. The fool is the one who vents all of it. Putting it off a few hours isn't what the verse describes.
Nothing in this verse says the wise man stores his anger up for a courtroom. It says he holds it back. The fool is the one letting it all out. Holding back is a different thing from stockpiling.
That one's flipped around, friend. The proverb says "If a ruler listens to lies, all his officials will be wicked." It says all, not a few. So it's false that only a few would go bad.

Right, it's false. The proverb says if a ruler listens to lies, all his officials will be wicked. That's every one of them, not just a few. Whatever the ruler listens to, his officials end up following.

explanations.answer: The LORD gives light to the eyes of both
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. "The poor man and the oppressor have this in common: The LORD gives light to the eyes of both." Those two couldn't be further apart, and yet this one thing is the same for both. The verse says it plainly and I'll leave it there.

explanations.answer: Both of them will stand before the king
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't mention a king at all. What the poor man and the oppressor have in common is that the LORD gives light to the eyes of both. Kings show up in other verses of the chapter, but not in this one.

explanations.answer: Both of them live inside the same city
explanations.explanation: The proverb never says anything about where either one lives. It names one thing they share: the LORD gives light to the eyes of both. The common ground here is what the LORD gives, not an address.
Not quite. The proverb says this king's throne "will be established forever." Forever is a lot longer than one lifetime. So the claim that it lasts only for his lifetime is false.
That's right. The king who judges the poor with fairness has a throne that will be established forever. Forever doesn't stop at one lifetime. It's a big promise for fair judging.

Yes, friend. "A rod of correction imparts wisdom, but a child left to himself disgraces his mother." It's the child left to himself that the verse is talking about. The word is disgraces, and it's a heavy one.
Comforts is the opposite direction. The proverb says a child left to himself disgraces his mother. The comfort, if you want to find it, is in the first half, where a rod of correction imparts wisdom.

The verse doesn't say the child protects anyone. It says a child left to himself disgraces his mother. Protecting would be a very different outcome. Wisdom comes from the rod of correction in the first half.
That's it. When the wicked thrive, rebellion increases. The verse then adds that the righteous will see their downfall. So the wicked thriving isn't where the story ends, friend.
It would be nice if thriving wicked people brought peace, but the proverb says the opposite. When the wicked thrive, rebellion increases. Peace isn't what grows along with them.
Joy goes with the righteous flourishing back in verse 2, where the people rejoice. Here, when the wicked thrive, rebellion increases. Different rulers, different results.

explanations.answer: Rest and delight to your soul
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. "Discipline your son, and he will give you rest; he will bring delight to your soul." Rest and delight are the two things the verse names. Anybody who's ever wanted a quiet evening knows how good that sounds.
The proverb doesn't mention an inheritance. It says the son will give you rest and bring delight to your soul. What's promised is rest and delight, not money.
Fame isn't in this verse. The proverb says that the disciplined son will give you rest and bring delight to your soul. It's a quieter reward, but I think it's the better one.
That's the one. "But blessed is he who keeps the Law." The first half says where there is no vision, the people cast off restraint. The blessing goes to the one who keeps the Law.
The verse doesn't call the city's ruler blessed. It says blessed is he who keeps the Law. A person can rule a city and still not be the one this verse is talking about.
Friends are great, and I miss some of mine every day. But the verse doesn't count them. The blessing goes to he who keeps the Law.

explanations.answer: He understands but will not respond
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. "A servant cannot be corrected by words alone; though he understands, he will not respond." So the words get through, but nothing changes. The trouble isn't that he can't understand, it's that he doesn't respond.

explanations.answer: He cannot understand the words at all
explanations.explanation: The verse says the opposite. "Though he understands, he will not respond." The words land fine in his ears. What doesn't happen is the response.

explanations.answer: He forgets the words by the next morning
explanations.explanation: Forgetting isn't what the proverb says. It says he understands but will not respond. He remembers fine, as far as the verse goes. He just doesn't act on it.

It's the other way around, friend. The proverb says "There is more hope for a fool than for him." The him is the man who speaks in haste. So the fool has more hope than the hasty talker, which makes this one false.

That's right. The proverb says there is more hope for a fool than for the man who speaks in haste. That's a strong way to say how risky hasty words are. I've shouted a few things too fast myself, so I feel this one.
Yes, friend. "A servant pampered from his youth will bring grief in the end." Notice the words in the end. The verse says that is where it lands.
Wealth would be a happy ending, but that's not in the verse. A servant pampered from his youth brings grief in the end. The ending isn't the sweet part of this proverb.
I'd love some praise, but that's not what this verse hands out. The pampered servant brings grief in the end. It's grief that's waiting for him, friend, not applause.
That's right. "A man's pride will bring him low, but a humble spirit will obtain honor." Pride sends him down instead of up. The humble spirit gets the honor.
Pride can feel strong from the inside, friend, but the proverb says otherwise. A man's pride will bring him low. The strength talk doesn't show up in this verse.
The proverb doesn't say pride keeps anyone safe. It says a man's pride will bring him low. Safety is closer to the trust in the LORD that a few verses later sets a man securely on high.
Yes, it's true. "A humble spirit will obtain honor." It's the second half of the same verse that says pride brings a man low. Honor goes to the humble.
The proverb does say it. "A man's pride will bring him low, but a humble spirit will obtain honor." Honor goes to the humble spirit. Pride is the one that gets brought low.

explanations.answer: He is set securely on high
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. "The fear of man is a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is set securely on high." The fear of man is a snare, and trusting the LORD is the opposite. Set securely on high is a solid place to stand.
The verse doesn't promise that nobody ever criticizes him. It says whoever trusts in the LORD is set securely on high. That's a promise about where he stands, not about what people say.

explanations.answer: He is given a seat by the king
explanations.explanation: A king doesn't appear in this verse. It says whoever trusts in the LORD is set securely on high. The place he's given comes from trusting the LORD, not from a ruler.
Yes, friend. "Many seek the ruler's favor, but a man receives justice from the LORD." The crowd is chasing the ruler, but justice comes from the LORD. That's the whole turn in the verse.
A crowd can shout loud, but the verse doesn't say justice comes from it. A man receives justice from the LORD. The crowd is closer to the many who seek the ruler's favor.
Priests don't appear anywhere in this chapter. The verse says a man receives justice from the LORD. Many seek the ruler's favor, but the justice comes from somewhere else.

That's right. "An unjust man is detestable to the righteous, and one whose way is upright is detestable to the wicked." Each side finds the other detestable. It's the chapter's last word, and the two groups just keep standing opposite each other.

explanations.answer: He is a friend to them
explanations.explanation: A friend is the opposite of what the verse says. One whose way is upright is detestable to the wicked. The unjust and the upright don't end up as friends here.

explanations.answer: He is a mystery to them
explanations.explanation: The proverb doesn't call him a mystery. It says the upright man is detestable to the wicked. They know exactly what they think of him, friend.
